quests.instruction: Arrange the four sentences into one clear paragraph.
quests.essayTopic: Describe why a short morning walk is worth adding to your day
options: A short walk each morning is one of the easiest ways to start the day well.
A habit that small costs almost nothing and keeps paying back until evening.
It gives the body gentle exercise before the day fills up with sitting.
Twenty minutes around the block, for instance, is often enough to feel awake by the time breakfast is ready.
quests.hint: Start with the sentence that tells the reader what the whole paragraph is about, then look for the one that gives a specific case of the reason.
quests.explanation: The opening sentence makes the claim the rest of the paragraph has to support. The reason explains why the claim holds, and only then does the twenty-minute example land, because it shows that reason at work. The closing thought steps back to the payoff; placed earlier, it would end the paragraph before any support had arrived.
quests.thesisStatement: A short morning walk is an easy, low-cost way to start the day well.

quests.instruction: Put these paragraph plans in the order a reader would expect.
quests.essayTopic: Reflect on what your first month in a new job taught you
options: Introduce the new job and say that the first month taught you one lesson you did not expect.
Describe the afternoon a quick question to a coworker fixed a mistake you had been carrying for days.
Explain the lesson: asking questions early saves more time than struggling alone.
Close by saying how you plan to use that lesson in every new task.
quests.hint: An essay tells the reader what is coming, develops it, and ends by looking ahead. Decide which plan is doing each of those jobs.
quests.explanation: A reader needs to know what the essay is about before meeting its content, so the introduction opens. The lesson is the central idea, and the afternoon story works better once the reader knows what it is meant to show. The conclusion goes last because it looks beyond the story to what the writer will do next.
quests.thesisStatement: Asking questions early in a new job saves more time than struggling silently.

quests.instruction: Order the moments of this story so the reader can follow what happened.
quests.essayTopic: Describe how you learned to ride a bicycle
options: Then one evening I stopped staring at the ground and looked toward the end of the road, and the bike steadied.
By the time the streetlights came on, I was riding loops around the car park on my own.
For weeks I wobbled along the empty car park, gripping the handlebars so hard my hands ached.
I was seven and convinced that balancing on two wheels was a trick reserved for older children.
quests.hint: In a story, each event should grow out of the one before it. Ask which moment has to have happened before the next one makes sense.
quests.explanation: Narrative writing follows time and cause together. The belief that riding is impossible comes first, the wobbling grows out of that belief, and the change in attention only matters after the struggle. The result is the payoff of that change, so it closes the story.
quests.thesisStatement: Learning to ride a bicycle depended on a change in attention rather than on strength or luck.

quests.instruction: Build a short explanatory paragraph that starts with the term and ends with why it matters.
quests.essayTopic: Explain what a household budget is and why a family needs one
options: With that plan already in place, an unexpected repair bill becomes a problem to manage rather than a crisis.
A household budget is a plan for how the money coming in each month will be spent.
It lists what arrives, what must be paid, and what is left over for everything else.
A family on a fixed salary might set aside amounts for rent, food, and savings before spending on anything else.
quests.hint: Explanatory writing usually names an idea, unpacks it, shows it working, and then says what it achieves. Which sentence is doing which job?
quests.explanation: Naming the term comes first because every later sentence depends on it. The definition unpacks the term, and the family example only makes sense once the reader knows what a budget contains. The last sentence explains the purpose, which is easiest to grasp after seeing the budget in use.
quests.thesisStatement: A household budget gives a family a clear plan that makes money decisions calmer and more deliberate.

quests.instruction: Arrange the paragraph so the answer follows the question it responds to.
quests.essayTopic: Discuss why some readers still prefer printed books
options: There are no notifications, no battery warnings, and no other apps waiting one tap away.
Why do so many readers still choose paper over a screen?
For readers who want to lose themselves in a story, that simplicity can matter more than convenience.
The main reason is that a printed book asks for nothing except attention.
quests.hint: Look for the sentence that raises the issue, the one that answers it, and the one that develops the answer before the writer draws a wider point.
quests.explanation: A question creates an expectation, so it opens the paragraph and the direct answer follows. The list of missing distractions is evidence for that answer, which is why it comes after it. The final sentence widens from the detail to what it means for readers, so it works as the implication rather than another detail.
quests.thesisStatement: Printed books remain popular because they protect a reader's attention.

quests.instruction: Trace the chain from cause to consequence to lesson.
quests.essayTopic: Explain how too little sleep affects a student's school day
options: Students who sleep too little arrive at school already tired.
A student who drifts off during a maths demonstration may spend that evening teaching herself the lesson from scratch.
A tired mind struggles to hold attention, so explanations slip past without being absorbed.
Protecting sleep protects learning as much as any revision session does.
quests.hint: Ask what has to be true before each sentence can make sense: what starts the problem, what it does to learning, and how one student experiences it.
quests.explanation: The paragraph works as a chain. Tiredness is the starting condition, weakened attention is what tiredness produces, and the student drifting off is a concrete case of that weakened attention. The lesson comes last because it is a conclusion drawn from the whole chain, not a fact the chain depends on.
quests.thesisStatement: Chronic lack of sleep undermines learning, so protecting sleep is part of protecting study.

quests.instruction: Arrange these paragraph plans into a complete essay outline.
quests.essayTopic: Explain how to prepare for a job interview
options: Open by saying that confidence in an interview comes mostly from preparation, not personality.
Show how rehearsing answers aloud turns that knowledge into calm, clear speech.
Close by reminding readers that preparation, not luck, shapes the first impression.
Explain how learning about the company lets candidates answer with specific knowledge.
quests.hint: Think about what a candidate must have before rehearsing is useful, and what the essay must establish before it moves into details.
quests.explanation: The introduction sets the essay's claim about preparation, so both body sections can serve it. Research comes before practice because rehearsal needs something worth saying; practising empty answers would not build the confidence the essay promises. The conclusion returns to the opening claim once both stages have been explained.
quests.thesisStatement: Interview confidence is built through preparation: researching the company, then practising answers aloud.

quests.instruction: Shape the opening so it moves from a familiar observation to the essay's claim.
quests.essayTopic: Discuss what makes someone a good neighbour
options: The paragraphs that follow look at three small habits that make that attention easy.
Yet when a pipe bursts or a parcel goes missing, neighbours are usually the first to notice.
Most people can name the street they live on but not the people who live beside them.
A good neighbour, in this sense, is defined less by friendliness than by quiet attention to the people nearby.
quests.hint: Which sentence would a reader need to have read before the claim feels earned, and which one only looks ahead to what the essay will do?
quests.explanation: The familiar observation invites the reader in, and the complication shows why it matters. Only then does the central claim have something to answer. The roadmap sentence goes last because it promises what the body will do, which only makes sense after the claim has been made.
quests.thesisStatement: A good neighbour is defined less by friendliness than by quiet attention to the people nearby.

quests.instruction: Order these steps so each one prepares the ground for the next.
quests.essayTopic: Explain how to build a study timetable you will actually follow
options: After a week, check which sessions you kept and move the ones you keep skipping.
A study timetable only works if it fits the life you already have.
Place study sessions in the gaps that remain, giving harder subjects the hours when you are most alert.
Write down the fixed parts of the week, such as classes, meals, and travel time.
quests.hint: Ask which step cannot be done until another is finished, and where a plan naturally checks its own results.
quests.explanation: The opening statement sets the standard the steps must meet. Listing fixed commitments has to happen before study sessions can be placed, because the sessions go into whatever time is left. Reviewing the plan comes last, since it can only judge a timetable that has already been tried.
quests.thesisStatement: A study timetable succeeds when it is built around real commitments and adjusted after a trial week.

quests.instruction: Build the argument so the reasons follow the stance they support.
quests.essayTopic: Argue that every adult should know basic first aid
options: A single weekend course can prepare an ordinary person to be useful in the worst minutes of someone else's day.
Someone who has already practised stopping bleeding or checking breathing is far more likely to stay calm enough to act.
Basic first aid is a skill every adult should have.
Emergencies rarely wait for a professional, and the first few minutes often matter most.
quests.hint: Find the sentence that takes a position. The reasons should build on each other: one shows the need, the next shows how training meets it.
quests.explanation: The position comes first so both reasons have something to defend. The urgency reason establishes the need, and the preparedness reason answers it; reversed, the talk of practised calm would arrive before the reader knows why calm matters. The final sentence turns the argument into something achievable.
quests.thesisStatement: Every adult should learn basic first aid because the first minutes of an emergency matter and training makes calm action possible.

quests.instruction: Organise this paragraph so the solution grows out of the problem.
quests.essayTopic: Suggest a practical way for a class to reduce noise at the start of lessons
options: The noise comes mostly from students who arrive at different times and have nothing to do while they wait.
Lessons in our classroom often lose their first ten minutes to chatter.
Lessons could then begin on time, and latecomers would slip into a working room instead of a noisy one.
A short warm-up question on the board, answered silently, would give every arrival something to do straight away.
quests.hint: A solution only makes sense once the reader knows what it is meant to fix. Track how the cause connects to the remedy.
quests.explanation: The problem is stated first so the reader knows what needs fixing. The cause narrows it: idle waiting is what produces the noise. The warm-up task answers that specific cause, which is why it follows, and the final sentence shows the result of the change.
quests.thesisStatement: A silent warm-up task would reduce start-of-lesson noise by giving arriving students something purposeful to do.

quests.instruction: Arrange this reflection so the lesson comes out of the experience.
quests.essayTopic: Reflect on what a group project taught you about communication
options: I learned that silence in a team usually means unshared assumptions rather than agreement.
In future projects, I will suggest a five-minute check-in halfway through the work.
Nobody asked, and two days before the deadline we discovered that we had each written the same section.
For our history presentation, four of us split the work and agreed to meet only if someone had a question.
quests.hint: Follow the experience as it unfolds, then look for the point where the writer steps back to interpret it.
quests.explanation: The reader needs the plan before the failure, and the failure before the lesson. The lesson only reads as earned once the duplicated sections have shown what silence hid. The final sentence turns that understanding into a specific change.
quests.thesisStatement: Group work fails quietly when teammates assume agreement, so brief check-ins are essential.

quests.instruction: Place each sentence where it helps the argument most.
quests.essayTopic: Argue that schools should teach basic personal budgeting
options: A first part-time pay cheque, for example, arrives with tax and deductions that few teenagers expect.
Money decisions begin early, usually before young people have received any real guidance.
Basic budgeting should be a regular part of the school curriculum.
Many students leave school able to solve equations but unsure how to compare two phone contracts.
quests.hint: Decide which sentence sets the scene, which states what the writer wants, and which goes on to justify and illustrate it.
quests.explanation: The gap between maths skills and money skills creates the need, so it opens. The claim then answers that need directly. The reason explains why the answer is urgent, and the pay cheque example makes that reason concrete, which is why it comes after rather than before it.
quests.thesisStatement: Schools should teach basic personal budgeting because young people face money decisions before they have guidance.

quests.instruction: Rebuild the outline so every supporting detail sits under the idea it belongs to.
quests.essayTopic: Explain how a small café can keep customers coming back
options: A small café keeps customers by making each visit feel personal.
Remembering names and usual orders shows regulars that they are noticed.
An owner who has a regular's coffee ready before they reach the counter offers attention no chain can copy.
Once customers feel known, small rewards such as a stamp card or early news of a new menu give them another reason to return.
quests.hint: Sort the ideas by level: which one covers the whole outline, which are sub-ideas, and which one only illustrates a sub-idea?
quests.explanation: An outline moves from the widest idea to narrower ones. The main idea governs everything. The owner's coffee example illustrates the point about remembering orders, so it must stay next to that point instead of being pushed down. The rewards build on customers already feeling known, so they form the second point.
quests.thesisStatement: A small café keeps regular customers by making each visit personal through recognition and modest rewards.

quests.instruction: Sequence this recommendation from the situation to a first practical step.
quests.essayTopic: Recommend how a club could welcome new members
options: New members often stand at the edge of the room because nobody has told them what to do.
The club should pair each newcomer with a friendly guide for their first month.
At the next intake, current members could sign up at the same table where newcomers register.
A guide can make introductions, explain routines, and keep the first meetings from feeling like a closed conversation.
quests.hint: A recommendation persuades best when the reader sees the need first, then the proposal, then the reasoning, and finally how to begin.
quests.explanation: The situation makes the reader care about a problem. The recommendation answers it, and the justification explains why that answer would work. The starting step comes last because it is only useful once the reader agrees the idea is worth trying.
quests.thesisStatement: Pairing each new member with a guide would make the club more welcoming from the first meeting.

quests.instruction: Follow the chain of events and put each consequence after what causes it.
quests.essayTopic: Explain how one late bus can spoil a school day
options: By lunchtime, a delay she did not cause has left her behind in one subject and frustrated in all of them.
When the morning bus arrives fifteen minutes late, a student reaches the gate just as registration closes.
Marked as late, she is sent to the office to sign in and misses the opening of her first lesson.
Without those opening instructions, she spends the rest of the class guessing what the task actually is.
quests.hint: Each event should be the reason the next one can happen. Test each pair: does the second only happen because of the first?
quests.explanation: A causal chain must run in the order the events depend on each other. The late arrival triggers the sign-in, the sign-in causes the missed instructions, and the missed instructions produce the confusion. The outcome sums up the whole chain and cannot come earlier without the reader missing how it happened.
quests.thesisStatement: A small transport delay can trigger a chain of missed information that affects a whole school day.

quests.instruction: Arrange the paragraph from claim to consequence.
quests.essayTopic: Discuss how deadlines can help creative work
options: A songwriter with a recording session on Friday picks a chorus instead of rewriting it for another month.
They force decisions that unlimited time allows a person to postpone forever.
Deadlines can be the friend of creative work rather than its enemy.
Limits turn a cloud of possibilities into something that can actually be finished.
quests.hint: Ask which sentence states the point, which explains why it holds, which shows it in a real case, and which widens the view again.
quests.explanation: The claim is surprising, so it needs an explanation before an illustration. The reason names the mechanism, the songwriter shows it in action, and the last sentence generalises from the case. Putting the example before the reason would show a behaviour before explaining what it demonstrates.
quests.thesisStatement: Deadlines help creative work by forcing decisions that turn possibilities into finished pieces.

quests.instruction: Order the sentences so the second idea is introduced through the first.
quests.essayTopic: Explain the difference between a goal and a habit
options: If you set a goal, attach it to one small daily action so the plan does not depend on enthusiasm.
A goal names something you want to reach, such as running a ten-kilometre race.
Goals tell you where to head, while habits decide whether you ever leave the house.
A habit is what you actually do each day, in that direction, whether or not you feel motivated.
quests.hint: Watch how one term is defined and the other is tied back to it. The relationship should come only once both terms are on the table.
quests.explanation: The habit sentence points back to the goal with its reference to direction, so the goal has to be defined first. The comparison of the two terms needs both definitions in place. Advice comes last because it applies the contrast to the reader's own plans.
quests.thesisStatement: A goal gives direction, but only daily habits turn that direction into progress.

quests.instruction: Arrange the paragraph so each supporting idea builds on the last.
quests.essayTopic: Discuss why cities plant trees along their streets
options: Shaded streets tend to invite people outside, and pavements with people on them feel safer than empty ones.
A row of trees is quietly part of how a neighbourhood looks after those who live there.
Trees along a street do more than decorate it.
Their leaves shade the pavement, which makes walking on a summer afternoon far more bearable.
quests.hint: Look for a cause that is later followed by a consequence, then a sentence that widens the point rather than adding another detail.
quests.explanation: Shade comes first because the second benefit depends on it: people only stay outside longer once the street is comfortable. The last sentence does not add another benefit; it draws a wider meaning from both, which is why it closes the paragraph.
quests.thesisStatement: Street trees improve a neighbourhood by cooling the pavement, drawing people outdoors, and making streets feel safer.

quests.instruction: Plan the paragraphs of this application essay so the story leads to the goal.
quests.essayTopic: Write a scholarship essay explaining why you want to study nursing
options: Explain how that night turned worry into curiosity about how caregivers stay steady.
Describe the volunteer hours that tested whether the interest was real.
Open with the night you helped your grandmother after her fall.
Finish by linking those experiences to the work you hope to do after training.
quests.hint: In a personal essay, the writer's interest should grow in stages. Decide which plan starts the story and which one needs earlier events to make sense.
quests.explanation: The essay begins with a specific moment because it gives the reader a reason to care. The curiosity grows out of that moment, and the volunteer hours only count as a test once there is an interest to test. The link to the future comes last because it uses everything before it as evidence.
quests.thesisStatement: Caring for my grandmother sparked an interest in nursing that volunteering has since proved genuine.

quests.instruction: Order this evaluation so the limitation qualifies the point before the advice.
quests.essayTopic: Evaluate how reliable online reviews are when buying a product
options: However, a handful of angry or paid comments can drag an average score away from the truth.
They often reveal problems that a product page never mentions.
Reading the middling reviews is often wiser, since those buyers tend to describe both the strengths and the flaws.
Online reviews are a useful starting point but not a final verdict.
quests.hint: Consider how the writer moves from a balanced claim to what supports it, what limits it, and what a reader should do because of both.
quests.explanation: The claim promises a balance, so the support and the limitation follow in that order: value first, then the caution. The advice comes last because it responds to both sides at once, recommending a way to gain the benefit while avoiding the risk.
quests.thesisStatement: Online reviews are a useful starting point for buying decisions but should not be treated as a final verdict.

quests.instruction: Narrow the opening step by step until it lands on a claim.
quests.essayTopic: Explain how a hobby can turn into a useful skill
options: Some pastimes, though, quietly train abilities that employers value.
Getting one good picture often means scouting the location, waiting for the light, and rejecting frames that are only almost right.
Almost everyone has a pastime they pursue only for fun.
Photography, for instance, can build patience, planning, and an eye for detail.
quests.hint: Move from the widest statement to the narrowest. The last sentence should sit closest to real, observable detail.
quests.explanation: The paragraph funnels from all pastimes to those that build skills, then to one example, then to what that example looks like in practice. Each sentence narrows the one before, so reversing any pair would leave a general statement stranded after a specific one.
quests.thesisStatement: Photography shows how a casual hobby can build patience, planning, and attention to detail.

quests.instruction: Build the body paragraph from claim to explanation.
quests.essayTopic: Explain why short breaks improve long study sessions
options: Short breaks make long study sessions more productive.
That renewed focus is what separates a long session that achieves something from one that only takes a long time.
The pause gives attention a chance to recover, so each new stretch begins with more focus than a tired straight run would allow.
One common routine has students work for twenty-five minutes and then rest for five before starting again.
quests.hint: Separate what happens (the routine) from why it works, and save the sentence that ties everything back to the claim for last.
quests.explanation: Evidence shows what happens, and explanation says why it works; explaining before the routine has been described would leave the reader without anything to interpret. The final sentence returns to the claim, showing that the recovered focus is the reason for the productivity gain.
quests.thesisStatement: Short breaks make long study sessions more productive by restoring attention.

quests.instruction: Arrange the paragraph so the effects run from individuals to the whole team.
quests.essayTopic: Examine how noisy open-plan offices affect concentration
options: Quiet zones or agreed focus hours would protect deep work without giving up the openness the layout was meant to create.
Individual workers lose their train of thought and need several minutes to regain it after each interruption.
Across a whole team, those small losses add up to slower projects and a habit of working late to catch up.
In an open-plan office, every phone call and conversation travels across the room.
quests.hint: Begin with the condition, follow its consequences from the smallest scale to the largest, and finish with what could be done about it.
quests.explanation: The situation describes the cause of the problem. The individual effect comes before the team effect because the team-level cost is the sum of many small personal interruptions. The response comes last, as it addresses the problem after the reader understands its scale.
quests.thesisStatement: Noise in open-plan offices erodes individual concentration and team efficiency, so focus zones are needed.

quests.instruction: Arrange this comparison so each point leads naturally to the judgment.
quests.essayTopic: Compare using a paper map with following a phone app
options: A map shows the whole area at once, so travellers learn how places connect.
An app shrinks that view to the next turn, which is efficient but rarely leaves a mental picture.
For a daily commute the app wins on speed; for exploring a new city, the map leaves you knowing more.
A paper map and a phone app will both get you there, but they train different habits.
quests.hint: Find the sentence that announces the comparison, then check which of the two descriptions is built on the other. The verdict comes once both have been described.
quests.explanation: The framing sentence tells the reader the two tools will be contrasted. The app description refers back to the map's wide view, so the map has to be described first. The judgment weighs both and therefore closes the paragraph.
quests.thesisStatement: Apps are better for speed, but paper maps build a fuller understanding of a place.

quests.instruction: Draft the email so the request is supported before the courtesy.
quests.essayTopic: Write a short email asking a manager to approve a training course
options: I would like to ask for approval to attend the two-day spreadsheet course in March.
At the moment I build our monthly reports by hand, which takes most of a working day.
Thank you for considering this, and I am happy to discuss timing whenever suits you.
The course covers automation tools that could bring that work down to an hour or so.
quests.hint: Think about how a busy reader processes a request: what they must know first, what makes it reasonable, and how a message should end.
quests.explanation: Stating the request first tells the manager what decision is needed. The current problem gives a reason, and the course benefit only makes sense as an answer to that problem. A courteous close finishes the message once the case has been made.
quests.thesisStatement: Approving the spreadsheet course would save significant reporting time each month.

quests.instruction: Arrange this reflection so the story earns the insight.
quests.essayTopic: Reflect on what learning to bake bread taught you about patience
options: The first time I baked bread, I opened the oven after ten minutes because I could not stand waiting.
Patience, I now think, is less a personality trait than the discipline of leaving a process alone.
I realised that some things cannot be hurried by wanting them finished.
What came out was pale, dense, and cold in the middle.
quests.hint: A reflective essay moves from event to result to what the writer takes from it, and only then to a wider idea.
quests.explanation: The failed loaf only makes sense after we know the writer opened the oven too soon. The personal realisation is drawn from that result. The broader claim is the widest step and needs the personal one beneath it, so it closes the reflection.
quests.thesisStatement: Patience is the discipline of leaving a process alone, a lesson learned through baking bread.

quests.instruction: Order these plans to outline an argument that still deals with an obvious objection.
quests.essayTopic: Argue whether schools should start later in the morning
options: Present reasoning that adequate sleep improves attention and mood during morning lessons.
Introduce the problem of tired teenagers and state that later start times deserve serious consideration.
Address the difficulties of bus timetables and after-school activities, and explain how schools could adapt to them.
Conclude that the benefits justify a trial, provided the schedule changes are managed carefully.
quests.hint: A persuasive plan usually builds its case before testing it against a difficulty. Decide where the objection strengthens the argument rather than interrupting it.
quests.explanation: The introduction frames the problem and position. The case for change must come before the objection so the reader knows what is being defended; otherwise the difficulties would be raised against a proposal not yet justified. The conclusion, which weighs benefits against a manageable cost, needs both sections to have appeared.
quests.thesisStatement: Schools should trial later start times because better sleep improves learning, and the scheduling problems can be managed.

quests.instruction: Arrange this paragraph so the claim, its support, and its limit are all in place.
quests.essayTopic: Evaluate whether language-learning apps are enough on their own
options: Most drill vocabulary and short sentences with remarkable consistency.
What they rarely provide is unscripted conversation, where a learner must understand and reply in real time.
That repetition builds the solid base of words and patterns that beginners lack.
Language apps are a strong way to begin but rarely enough on their own.
quests.hint: Follow the logic of a balanced judgment: what is offered, why that is valuable, and what remains missing.
quests.explanation: The qualified claim promises both strengths and a limit. The drilling is the evidence, and its explanation needs that evidence first. The limitation closes the paragraph because it delivers the second half of the claim, the reason apps are not enough.
quests.thesisStatement: Language apps give beginners a solid base but cannot replace real-time conversation.

quests.instruction: Sequence the argument so the complication reshapes the claim.
quests.essayTopic: Discuss whether technology makes friendships easier to maintain
options: Technology makes friendships easier to maintain, but not automatically easier to keep strong.
Messaging apps let friends in different cities trade news every day.
Yet frequent contact is not the same as closeness, and a stream of short messages can crowd out the long conversations where friendships deepen.
The sensible response is to treat messages as a bridge to calls and visits rather than a replacement for them.
quests.hint: Ask what evidence of convenience the writer starts from, what qualifies it, and which sentence only makes sense once both have been stated.
quests.explanation: The observation establishes the convenience side, and the complication then complicates it. The nuanced claim is a balance of both and cannot be stated before them. The implication gives practical direction based on that balanced claim.
quests.thesisStatement: Technology makes friendships easier to maintain but not automatically stronger.
